ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. Incidental calcified granuloma, benign.

contraindications: Migraine with aura, at any age: UKMEC category 4 and WHO MEC category 4 (unacceptable health risk) for all combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch, ring), because oestrogen adds to the raised risk of ischaemic stroke associated with aura (UKMEC 2025; WHO MEC 5th edition 2015).
interactions: Paracetamol (current as-needed analgesic): no clinically relevant interaction.
Sumatriptan and other triptans: no clinically relevant interaction with combined oral contraceptives; no dose change needed.
output.summary: Oestrogen-containing contraception is category 4 in migraine with aura; progestogen-only and intrauterine methods are category 1 or 2.
warnings: Drospirenone-containing combined pills carry a higher venous thromboembolism risk than levonorgestrel-containing pills.
Switch without a gap in contraceptive cover.

output.query: migraine aura with visual then sensory symptoms and numbness

results.finding: Visual symptoms occurred in almost all people with migraine aura and sensory symptoms in about a third; when several aura symptoms occurred they usually followed one another rather than starting together.
results.source: Russell MB, Olesen J. A nosographic analysis of the migraine aura in a general population. Brain 1996;119:355-361

results.finding: Sensory aura is typically pins and needles moving slowly from the point of origin, but numbness may be the only symptom; when symptoms occur in succession each may last up to 60 minutes.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211 (1.2.1 Migraine with typical aura)

output.summary: Sensory aura, including pure numbness, follows visual aura in a substantial minority of attacks and is part of typical aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two attacks of left visual scintillation spreading over 15-20 minutes followed by left hand and cheek numbness, each resolving within 30 minutes, then right-sided migrainous headache: criteria A to D met with 6 of 6 C characteristics; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and apply ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A to D
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with aura is a clinical diagnosis; applying ICHD-3 to her two attacks establishes typical aura, and a normal examination with a stereotyped pattern means imaging is not required.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct or structural lesion; two punctate non-specific frontal subcortical hyperintensities
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI (optional: recent-onset typical aura with a normal examination)
action_criteria.rationale: A typical aura with a normal examination needs no imaging (Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336; AAN 2000); MRI is acceptable here because the aura is of recent onset and her father had a stroke at 45, and is preferred to CT.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Yasmin identified as category 4 under UKMEC and WHO MEC because of the aura, with progestogen-only and intrauterine methods named as safe options
action_criteria.label: Check her combined oral contraceptive (Yasmin) against migraine with aura
action_criteria.rationale: She takes an oestrogen-containing pill. Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 2025 and WHO MEC 2015 category 4 in migraine with aura, so the check changes management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence that visual then sensory symptoms, including numbness, occur in typical aura
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on combined visual and sensory migraine aura (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis rests on the history and examination.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Stop Yasmin now: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; switch without a gap to a progestogen-only pill (desogestrel 75 micrograms), implant, levonorgestrel IUS or copper IUD.

Offer sumatriptan 50-100 mg taken at headache onset rather than during the aura, with an NSAID and an antiemetic such as metoclopramide 10 mg because the attacks cause vomiting, and keep triptan use to fewer than 10 days a month (NICE CG150).
Give a headache diary and review; preventive treatment is not indicated at two attacks in six weeks (AHS 2021).

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis; neither is present here

Echocardiography, including a bubble study for PFO, is not indicated in migraine with aura without stroke; PFO closure does not treat migraine (PREMIUM, Tobis JM et al., JACC 2017; PRIMA, Mattle HP et al., Eur Heart J 2016; MIST, Dowson A et al., Circulation 2008).

accepted: Migraine with combined visual and sensory aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); combined OCP contraindicated (WHO Category 4)

differential.key_features: Two stereotyped attacks with a positive visual symptom spreading over 15-20 minutes, sensory symptoms in succession and a migrainous headache, in a 29-year-old without vascular risk factors; negative sensory symptoms occur in typical aura.

Raised by migraine with aura and a father's stroke at 45, but the aura is typical and the MRI shows only two punctate frontal subcortical hyperintensities, with normal anterior temporal white matter and external capsules.

differential.diagnosis: Focal seizure with sensory and visual phenomena
differential.key_features: Seizure symptoms spread over seconds, not 15-20 minutes, and are not followed by a 12-14 hour migrainous headache.
MRI shows no abnormal flow voids, haemorrhage or haemosiderin; two attacks on the same side are too few to define a fixed-side pattern.

key_clinical_evidence: Two stereotyped attacks of left visual scintillation spreading over 15-20 minutes, followed in succession by left hand and cheek numbness, resolving within 30 minutes and followed by a migrainous headache: ICHD-3 1.2.1 with 6 of 6 C characteristics.
Numbness without tingling is a negative sensory symptom that occurs in typical aura; it does not by itself suggest TIA.
She takes Yasmin: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 with migraine aura and must be stopped.
Typical aura with a normal examination: imaging is optional; if done, MRI shows only two non-specific punctate white matter hyperintensities.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A parent's early stroke does not explain two stereotyped typical auras; it adds weight to stopping oestrogen-containing contraception. Thrombophilia testing and echocardiography are not indicated for migraine with aura.
red_herrings.intended_effect: May suggest an inherited cerebrovascular disorder or thrombophilia and prompt a stroke work-up

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Numbness occurs in typical sensory aura; here it followed a spreading visual aura in succession and preceded a migrainous headache.
red_herrings.data_point: Numbness of the left hand and cheek, a 'dead' feeling without tingling
red_herrings.intended_effect: Negative sensory symptom may anchor on TIA

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The attacks are brief, stereotyped and fully reversible with a normal examination and no persisting headache, fever or papilloedema; the trigger pattern is on-call stress.
red_herrings.data_point: Travel to Nigeria in hot weather two weeks before the first attack
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt a search for dehydration-related venous thrombosis or a travel-related infection

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Small non-specific subcortical hyperintensities are common in migraine with aura; the CADASIL regions (anterior temporal lobes, external capsules) are normal.
red_herrings.data_point: Two punctate frontal subcortical white matter hyperintensities on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt a demyelination or CADASIL work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history decides whether a red flag justifies imaging.

findings.result: Two stereotyped attacks in 6 weeks, both during on-call periods; none before.
Visual (shimmering, flickering area in the left visual field) followed by sensory (numbness of the left hand and left cheek). No weakness, speech or brainstem symptom. Fully reversible.
Visual area expanded slowly over 15-20 minutes.
Sensory symptom began during the second half of the visual aura.
Each symptom under 30 minutes; both resolved within 30 minutes.
Unilateral: left visual field, left hand and left cheek.
Visual scintillation. The sensory symptom was negative (numbness).
Severe right-sided pulsating headache after the aura, with nausea, vomiting and photophobia, lasting 12-14 hours.

Headache-free. Visual fields full to confrontation, no papilloedema, eye movements normal, power 5/5 without drift, sensation intact, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantars flexor, coordination and gait normal. BP 118/72 mmHg, afebrile.

Recent onset of a new headache type (6 weeks): present, with a stereotyped typical pattern. Systemic symptoms, history of neoplasm, persisting deficit, thunderclap onset, age over 50, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, progression, pregnancy or puerperium, painful eye, head trauma, immune suppression and analgesic overuse: absent.
Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms with drospirenone 3 mg) for 3 years. Non-smoker, no alcohol, no hypertension or heart disease. Father had a stroke at 45.

clinical_assessment.impression:
1. Two attacks of visual then sensory aura followed by migrainous headache: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A to D met, 6 of 6 C characteristics. Supports migraine with typical aura with headache (ICHD-3 1.2.1.1).
2. No persisting deficit, no motor, speech or brainstem aura; examination normal.

additional_observations: No restricted diffusion on DWI and ADC.
No haemorrhage or microhaemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
No mass, abnormal flow voids or cortical malformation.
Anterior temporal white matter and external capsules normal.
Ventricles, sulci and posterior fossa normal for age.

findings.location: Right frontal and left frontal subcortical white matter

mri.impression:
1. No acute infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion.
2. Two punctate frontal subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, non-specific.

metadata.condition_name: Migraine with combined visual and sensory aura: combined pill and a father's early stroke
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: recent-onset visual then sensory aura with a negative sensory symptom and a father's stroke at 45 invite a TIA or stroke work-up; the combined pill contraindication is the critical management point
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Moderate: combined pill discontinuation and vascular red herrings

patient.chief_complaint: Two episodes of left-sided visual disturbance with numbness and severe headache in past 6 weeks

family_history: Father had stroke at 45; mother 'always had bad headaches' (possible migraine); no family history of hemiplegic migraine or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Junior doctor (F1); non-smoker; no alcohol; single; high work stress; recent travel to Nigeria (2 months ago)

patient.history_present_illness:
A 29-year-old Nigerian-British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic with two episodes over the past 6 weeks of a similar disturbance. In both episodes, she first noticed a shimmering, flickering area in the left side of her visual field that slowly expanded over approximately 15-20 minutes. Simultaneously with the second half of the visual disturbance, she noticed numbness of her left hand and left cheek — a 'dead' feeling without tingling. Both symptoms resolved completely within 30 minutes and were followed by a severe right-sided pulsating headache (8/10) with nausea, vomiting, and severe photophobia lasting 12-14 hours.

She had never experienced anything like this before the first episode 6 weeks ago. She mentioned to her GP that she had visited Nigeria 8 weeks ago, where the weather was very hot — this was two weeks before the first episode. She has no cardiac disease and no hypertension. Her mother never mentioned migraines but 'always had bad headaches'. She is currently on the combined oral contraceptive pill (Yasmin — EE 30 mcg + drospirenone) and has been for 3 years. She is a junior doctor in her first year of training, and the episodes both occurred during very stressful on-call periods.

She is particularly concerned because her father had a stroke at age 45. She is a non-smoker, no alcohol. She is otherwise very healthy. She specifically denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any persisting visual loss.
